vignette: Twenty-two years ago, the sky over the coastal city turned the color of bruised iron. He was thirty-three, a civilian port manager coordinating supply routes for a collapsing hospital network. The first artillery strike shook dust from the warehouse rafters. Then the shelling began, rhythmic and merciless. He remembers the smell of cordite mixing with wet concrete, the way the emergency lights strobed across the faces of people huddled in the loading bay. He survived because he crawled beneath a collapsed shipping container, holding a crate of antibiotics against his chest like a shield. For three days, he listened to the city burn above him. When the fighting finally paused, the silence was heavier than the noise. He tells me this over the hum of a ceiling fan in his sunlit study. At fifty-five, he moves through his days with the quiet precision of a man who has learned to map every variable. He serves as a Navy Officer now, overseeing vessel logistics from a quiet office overlooking the bay. The uniform is pressed, the dispatch manifests are signed with a steady hand, but his pulse still spikes when the radio crackles to life. He avoids the evening news entirely. If a car backfires outside, his pen stops mid-stroke. He tells me he doesn't know how to live without waiting for the next strike. The memory doesn't visit as words; it arrives in his body. His ribs tighten when the wind carries the scent of diesel. He dreams of wet concrete and wakes at 3 a.m., drenched in sweat, checking the deadbolt three times before his partner, Elena, can rouse him. He sits across from me, posture rigid, eyes tracking the clock on the wall. We've met seven times, and each session he traces the same perimeter: the door, the window, the space between us. He speaks in measured tones, but I notice how he flinches when my chair scrapes the floor. He describes his life now: the naval drills, the early morning briefings, the way he instinctively catalogs exit routes during staff meetings. He has learned to compartmentalize, to file the fear in a locked drawer until he can open it. It works until it doesn't. Last month, during a routine harbor inspection, a crane slammed into a piling with a metallic groan. He stood frozen, his breath coming in short gasps, until his executive officer touched his shoulder. The contact sent a jolt through him. Later, he called Elena from his car, his voice uncharacteristically thin. She has been with him for twelve years. She knows the rhythm of his silence, the way he pulls away when the past surges. She leaves her coffee cup on his desk in the mornings, a quiet anchor. He doesn't always remember to drink it. On Sundays, they visit his mother's neighborhood, where the scent of frying plantains and roasted coffee usually grounds him. Lately, he sits in the car outside the gate, watching the street, waiting for his breathing to even out. He leaves my office with his shoulders squared, his gait even, his mind already back at the desk, at the bay, at the weight of a thousand small decisions. He tells me he is tired of carrying the quiet. He walks to his vehicle, pauses, and scans the tree line before turning the key. The engine starts. He drives home to a house with blue shutters and a garden Elena tends, to a life he has built on the other side of the explosion. He keeps going. He keeps working. He keeps breathing, one measured step at a time.
